facts.statement: Soroavisaurus lived in South America during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 71 to 69 million years ago.
facts.quote: Soroavisaurus is an extinct genus of enantiornithine birds that lived in South America during the Late Cretaceous period, about 71–69 million years ago.

facts.statement: Soroavisaurus lived in the Maastrichtian age on a warm, humid coastal plain featuring tropical forests, ponds, and lagoons.
facts.quote: The Lecho Formation dates to the Maastrichtian age and was deposited on a warm, humid coastal plain with tropical forests, ponds and lagoons.

facts.statement: The species Soroavisaurus australis was named in 1993.
facts.quote: The only known species, Soroavisaurus australis, was named in 1993

facts.statement: All known specimens of Soroavisaurus are fossilized leg bones found at El Brete in the Salta province of Argentina.
facts.quote: All specimens confidently assigned to this species are fossilised leg bones collected from the Lecho Formation of El Brete, a locality in the province of Salta, Argentina.

facts.statement: The fossil deposits of the Lecho Formation at El Brete were discovered in 1975 by a team from the Fundación Miguel Lillo.
facts.quote: In 1975, fossil-bearing deposits of the Lecho Formation were discovered at the locality of El Brete, Salta Province, Argentina by a team from the Fundación Miguel Lillo.

facts.statement: In 1981, Cyril Walker identified the bird fossils from El Brete as belonging to the group Enantiornithes.
facts.quote: In 1981, British paleontologist Cyril Walker published a study in which he illustrated some of these bones and determined that while they represent multiple species, all of them would have been members of a group which he named the Enantiornithes.

facts.statement: The holotype of Soroavisaurus is the left tarsometatarsus specimen PVL-4690.
facts.quote: He designated a left tarsometatarsus with the specimen number PVL-4690 as the holotype of this species

facts.statement: Soroavisaurus is estimated to have been about 40 cm long, though size variation suggests some individuals were larger.
facts.quote: The body length of Soroavisaurus has been estimated at about 40 cm, but the disparity in size among known specimens suggests that some individuals grew larger than others.

facts.statement: Soroavisaurus belongs to the bird family Avisauridae.
facts.quote: Soroavisaurus is a member of the family Avisauridae

facts.statement: All known fossils of Soroavisaurus consist exclusively of hind limb bones.
facts.quote: All known specimens of Soroavisaurus preserve only bones from the hind limbs.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen PVL-4690 is a left tarsometatarsus measuring 46.9 mm in length.
facts.quote: The holotype, PVL-4690, is a 46.9 mm long left tarsometatarsus.

facts.statement: Specimen PVL-4048 includes a 51.5 mm left tarsometatarsus associated with the hallux and four toe bones.
facts.quote: A larger specimen, PVL-4048, includes another left tarsometatarsus, which is 51.5 mm long and associated with the whole hallux (digit I) and four intermediate phalanges (toe bones).

facts.statement: The Soroavisaurus tarsometatarsus is a slender bone formed by the fusion of tarsal and metatarsal bones only in the upper portion.
facts.quote: The tarsometatarsus is slender and formed from the fusion of the tarsal and metatarsal bones, though the metatarsals of Soroavisaurus are fused only in the proximal (upper) portion.

facts.statement: Metatarsal IV is flattened and slender, creating a distinct gap between it and metatarsal III in the upper part of the tarsometatarsus.
facts.quote: Metatarsal IV is weaker than the other two as it is flattened and slender, particularly in its proximal half, such that a gap is formed between it and metatarsal III in the upper part of the tarsometatarsus.

facts.statement: The gap between metatarsals III and IV is a unique defining feature of Soroavisaurus not found in other enantiornithines.
facts.quote: This gap is a defining feature of Soroavisaurus and is not present in any other known enantiornithine bird.

facts.statement: The trochlea of metatarsal IV has a triangular outline with a bony projection that nearly seals the gap between metatarsals III and IV.
facts.quote: The trochlea of metatarsal IV has a vaguely triangular outline when viewed from below, with a bony projection on the inner edge which almost seals a small gap between metatarsals III and IV.

facts.statement: The first toe (digit I) consists of two phalanges forming a sharp, curved talon.
facts.quote: Digit I is formed by two phalanx bones; the one joined to metatarsal I has a swollen articular surface that joins to the other phalanx, which in turn forms a sharp, curved talon.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Soroavisaurus is the same species as Enantiornis or Martinavis, though confirmation is difficult due to the lack of overlapping fossil parts.
facts.quote: Some authors have proposed that either Enantiornis or Martinavis, which are known from wing bones found at the same locality, may represent the same animal as Soroavisaurus. However it is difficult to confirm which (if either) of these truly is the same species.

facts.statement: A 2007 study suggested that Soroavisaurus might be a junior synonym of Enantiornis.
facts.quote: In a study published in 2007, it was suggested that Soroavisaurus may be a junior synonym of Enantiornis, which is known from the same locality.

facts.statement: Researchers note that it is difficult to determine if wing fossils belong to Soroavisaurus, and some suggest a Martinavis species might represent its wings instead of Enantiornis.
facts.quote: However, the authors acknowledge that it is difficult to determine which (if any) of the El Brete enantiornithines known only from wing bones represent the same species as any of those known only from leg bones, and that one of the Martinavis species (rather than Enantiornis) may instead represent the wings of Soroavisaurus.

facts.statement: The exact position of Soroavisaurus within the family Avisauridae is debated, with some authors placing it as an early-diverging member rather than close to North American forms like Avisaurus.
facts.quote: Soroavisaurus is a member of the family Avisauridae, but its exact position within this family has been debated; the North American forms Avisaurus and Gettyia were originally thought to be its closest relatives, but other South American forms like Intiornis were later proposed to be closer to it, and some authors place Soroavisaurus as an early-diverging member of the family.

facts.statement: Soroavisaurus is classified as an extinct member of the avian clade Enantiornithes.
facts.quote: Soroavisaurus belongs to an extinct clade of avialans (birds, in a broad sense) known as the Enantiornithes.

facts.statement: Soroavisaurus is placed in the family Avisauridae as a close relative of the North American genus Avisaurus.
facts.quote: Within this clade, it has been determined to be a close relative of the North American Avisaurus, and has therefore been placed alongside it in the family Avisauridae.

facts.statement: A 2024 study revised the family Avisauridae to include only six members, excluding genera previously thought to belong to it.
facts.quote: A 2024 publication revised the classification of Avisauridae and retained only six members in the family, excluding other genera that were formerly considered members of this group.

facts.statement: Recent research suggests Intiornis is a more basal relative of the group leading to Avisauridae rather than the closest relative of Soroavisaurus.
facts.quote: With this revision, Intiornis was no longer deemed the closest relative of Soroavisaurus, and instead was considered a more basal (earlier-diverging) member of a group leading to Avisauridae.

facts.statement: Soroavisaurus is considered to occupy a basal position within the family Avisauridae.
facts.quote: Meanwhile, Soroavisaurus was retained in a basal position within Avisauridae.

facts.statement: The genus Soroavisaurus was named by Luis M. Chiappe in 1993.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Chiappe, 1993

facts.statement: The only known species, Soroavisaurus australis, is known from fossils collected from the Lecho Formation in Estancia El Brete, southern Salta Province, Argentina.
facts.quote: La única especie conocida, S. australis, es conocida a partir de fósiles recolectados de la Formación Lecho (etapa del Maastrichtiense) en Estancia El Brete, en el extremo sur de la provincia de Salta, Argentina.

facts.statement: The fossil record includes specimen PVL-4690, a left tarsometatarsus 46.9 mm long, and PVL-4048, a left tarsometatarsus 51.5 mm long associated with an incomplete hallux and four intermediate phalanges.
facts.quote: Son catalogados como PVL-4690, un tarsometatarso izquierdo de 46.9 milímetros de largo, y PVL-4048, el cual incluye a otro tarsometatarso izquierdo de 51.5 mm de largo asociado con un hallux incompleto, el dígito I, y cuatro falanges intermedias.

facts.statement: Specimen PVL-4048 was previously described as "Avisaurus sp." before being assigned to Soroavisaurus.
facts.quote: PVL-4048 fue anteriormente descrito como "Avisaurus sp." (véase Avisaurus).

facts.statement: All known specimens of Soroavisaurus come from the Maastrichtian age of the Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: All known specimens of Soroavisaurus originate from exposures of the Lecho Formation at the locality of El Brete, which date back to the Maastrichtian age of the Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: The Lecho Formation deposits containing Soroavisaurus are estimated to be between 71 and 69 million years old.
facts.quote: More specifically, the age of the Lecho Formation has been estimated to be between 71 and 69 million years, so its deposits would have formed during the start or middle of the Maastrichtian.

facts.statement: The environment at El Brete where Soroavisaurus lived was a coastal plain dotted with ponds and lagoons.
facts.quote: Based on the type of sediment that these deposits are composed of, El Brete is believed to have been a coastal plain during that time, pockmarked with ponds and lagoons.

facts.statement: The habitat near the Tropic of Capricorn featured a humid, warm climate supporting coastal tropical forests.
facts.quote: In addition, the area would have been near the Tropic of Capricorn, giving it a humid and warm climate that supported coastal tropical forests.

facts.statement: Soroavisaurus is hypothesized to have been a perching carnivore occupying an ecological niche similar to modern birds of prey.
facts.quote: Based on its large size and strong talons, Soroavisaurus was likely a carnivore capable of perching, and has been hypothesized to occupy a similar ecological niche to extant birds of prey.

facts.statement: The time range for Soroavisaurus is estimated from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)
